title: Clachan-crìche cut and set along Roinn na Rìoghachd
summary: Through the winter after the handful the stewards of the nine lines ride the boundaries with the reciters, agreeing what they can, and masons cut and set the clachan-crìche, each stone bearing the sign of the share it faces. Some are moved in the night and set again by morning.

title: A stone set on each bank at Dùn thais
summary: No steward of the north or of an Earrann Dhearg will yield Dùn thais to the other, so the masons of both lines set a stone on the north bank of the burn below the old fort, cut with Murchadh's sign, and another on the south bank, cut with the sign of an Earrann Dhearg, and leave the hill itself between the two.

title: Ìomhar Dearg claims the grazing above Dùn thais
summary: At his own supper-table Ìomhar Dearg tells his grandson Ruairidh Glas that the grazing on the northern slope above Dùn thais belongs to an Earrann Dhearg, stone or no stone, and that it is time the cattle grazing there under the northern share's sign were driven off it.

title: Aonghas Bàn carried home to his brother's hall
summary: Ruairidh Glas's men carry Aonghas Bàn mac Mhurchaidh down off the hill of Dùn thais in a cloak between two spear-shafts, in the rain, and word runs ahead of them to his own household, where his brother Eachann Ruadh is already waiting at the gate.

title: Eachann Ruadh's oath over his brother's body
summary: Eachann Ruadh mac Mhurchaidh kneels by his brother's body in the yard of their own hall and swears that the blood spilt at Dùn thais will be answered, blood for blood, by his own hand or his sons' after him, without naming the man he means, which by the old custom of the households leaves the quarrel open to a settling short of a second death.

title: Ìomhar Dearg refuses to answer for the killing
summary: Ìomhar Dearg tells his grandson Ruairidh Glas that he did no more than a man does when his own are threatened, and that he is not to trouble himself with an oath sworn by a boy over his brother's body. The line of Ìomhar makes no answer to Eachann Ruadh's oath.

title: The shares parted into countries and provinces
summary: Under each of na h-Earrannan Mòra the households sworn to it are parted again into countries, and the countries into provinces, as the lines of the king's dead children are fitted in among the living heirs' claims.

title: Provinces parted again into counties and holdings
summary: Below the provinces the land is cut finer still, into counties and, under the counties, holdings no larger than a single steading, sworn by whichever household holds them to whatever county's steward stands nearest and troubles to ride out and take the oath.

title: Holdings sworn to two counties and to three
summary: A stream that shifts its bed in a wet winter leaves more than one holding claimed by two counties at once, and some households, rather than fight for the difference, swear to both and pay both, and the two counties are slow to compare their rolls.

title: The three lords of the mill on the Abhainn dhomhain
summary: Three counties meeting at a bend of the Abhainn dhomhain each claim the eel-catch of an old mill's pond, and the miller, who built the wheel before Roinn na Rìoghachd was thought of, takes to paying each lord a third of the autumn catch unasked, and the quarrel goes no further.

title: Luchd nan Snaidhm count forty-four countries
summary: Riding the boundaries themselves with cords of their own, Luchd nan Snaidhm of Dùn ìseal come to a count of forty-four countries under na h-Earrannan Mòra, a count that holds for a season before two countries are found to have quietly divided themselves into three apiece.

title: The count of a hundred and thirty-one provinces
summary: Luchd nan Snaidhm count a hundred and thirty-one provinces under the countries, and hold the number the better part of a year, though even as it is counted two provinces of Earrann Caol shean split into three over a fishing-weir.

title: Luchd nan Snaidhm give up the count at the counties
summary: Cairistìona, Sìne's eldest daughter, tells Aodh Crom that the counties change their own boundaries faster than any cord can be tied to hold them, and that a knot-keeper who tries to count them all will chase a number that is never the same twice. The count of counties is given up unfinished.

title: A boundary quarrel brought to Talla na Lasrach's ground
summary: Stewards of an Earrann Dhearg and Earrann Mhurchaidh, come to lay a raid and a cattle-theft before the keepers, nearly bring their quarrel armed onto the ground under the mountain. Aodh Crom stands between them and says again that no spear may come onto that ground in anger.

title: The heirs go home from the valley
summary: In the second summer after the stones went up at Dùn thais, the heirs and their households go home from the valley below Dùn ìseal, most of them for the first time in nearly two years without a boundary still openly disputed.
